comment: Pleroma / Sandalphon seccomp profile (2026-10 §CG, corrected §CI). defaultAction is SCMP_ACT_ALLOW (denylist style), NOT SCMP_ACT_ERRNO. A full allowlist (default-deny) profile would be the architecturally stronger design, but building one correctly requires exhaustively tracing every syscall the real python:3.11-alpine entrypoint needs for the full range of scripts this jail actually runs -- and that tracing requires running the real container, which this development environment's network allowlist blocks (container registries are unreachable here; see GRIMOIRE.md §CF). Guessing an allowlist blind risks silently breaking the sandbox's basic function in a way that would only surface later, which is the kind of unverified claim this project explicitly avoids. This denylist is therefore the honest, verifiable middle ground for now: it closes a documented, concrete set of dangerous primitives (process creation, ptrace, mount/namespace manipulation, kernel module and system control, privilege-related syscalls, raw networking as defense-in-depth on top of --network none, time tampering, NUMA/keyring exotica) without risking any legitimate script execution, since none of these syscalls appear in a baseline python interpreter startup+execution trace (confirmed via strace on this host). [§CI self-correction, discovered on real GitHub Actions infrastructure once Docker/registries first became reachable there] The original §CG version of this profile also denied execve/execveat, reasoning (wrongly) that a disposable script run never needs to replace its own process image. That reasoning only accounted for the already-running interpreter executing a script; it missed that Docker/runc loads this very seccomp filter onto the container's PID 1 BEFORE that process execve's into the configured ENTRYPOINT (`python`) -- so denying execve entirely prevented the container from ever starting at all (observed for real: `exec /usr/local/bin/python: operation not permitted`). execve/execveat are therefore deliberately left off this denylist. This does not meaningfully reopen the fork/exec escape path §CG was closing: fork/vfork/clone/clone3 remain denied below, and Linux cannot create a new process (whether via raw fork+exec, posix_spawn, or anything else) without first going through one of those syscalls, so a script already running inside this jail still cannot spawn any new process regardless of execve's own allow/deny status. Moving to a full allowlist is left as a documented follow-up for an environment where the real container image can actually be pulled and traced end-to-end (e.g. GitHub Actions).

syscalls.comment: Process creation. The jail runs one disposable script to completion and starting a brand-new process (fork/vfork/clone/clone3) has no legitimate use here -- this is also the kernel-level backstop for the os.fork/subprocess family that §CC and the audit-hook layers already police at the Python layer. execve/execveat are deliberately NOT included here (§CI correction): the container's own ENTRYPOINT (`python`) must execve under this very filter just to start, so denying execve breaks the jail's basic function rather than hardening it. Denying fork/vfork/clone/clone3 already blocks any new process from being created in the first place (posix_spawn and the os.exec family all require one of these first on Linux), which is the actual escape primitive this rule exists to close -- an already-running script being able to execve is not, by itself, a way to create a second process.
Process introspection / debugging. No legitimate script run in this jail needs to inspect or write into another process's memory.

Mount/filesystem-namespace manipulation. The jail's root filesystem is already --read-only; none of these operations are needed to run a script and all of them are classic container-escape primitives.
Kernel module / system-wide control. A disposable per-script container has no legitimate need to load kernel modules, reboot the host, or otherwise affect anything outside itself.

Namespace / privilege manipulation. --cap-drop=ALL (§CF) already makes most of these fail at the capability-check layer, but blocking them at the seccomp layer too is cheap defense-in-depth that fails earlier and does not depend on the capability check being correctly configured.

Raw networking, as defense-in-depth on top of --network none. AF_UNIX socket()/socketpair() do not require a network namespace and would otherwise still succeed inside this jail; blocking the whole socket-family syscall surface closes that gap rather than relying solely on there being no route.
Host clock/time tampering. No legitimate script run in this jail needs to change the system clock.
NUMA memory-policy manipulation and the kernel keyring. Historically exploit-prone, never needed by an ordinary disposable script.
Miscellaneous legacy syscalls with no legitimate use here.
